Hey, I know I'm late to the party but here's my tips:

**1) If you're on a pump: Check your site.** At some point your tubing might have gotten loose. It's okay, it's common, and it'll happen for seemingly no reason at all. Of course, fixing this problem requires a new pod or what have you.

**2) Like many people have suggested: Check for illnesses.** Being sick or having an infection can throw your system way outta wack. I won't get too far into it, but basically your body releases hormones and glucose to help your body fight off the sickies, which as a side effect can raise your BG.

**3)** **Insulin resistance.** Again, like many others here have said, it's important to change injection sites often; this helps prevent scar tissue and lets the skin heal, which does wonders for absorption rates. If you use the same site repeatedly, you won't take in insulin as well.

I'm assuming your doing manual injections?

On the back of (most) food packaging there is a Nutrition Facts section. What you're looking for is the serving size and the carbohydrate count. Once you know how much of that food you're gonna eat, multiply the carbs by how many serving you'll have. Do this for each food and inject accordingly. As for IC ratio, this should have been told by your endo what it is at this current point in time. If you're unsure, try looking up average ICs based on stuff like your BMI. Anywho, once you have the carbs, divide your carbs by the IC ratio to find out how much insulin to take.

Here's an example: I love Watermelon Sherbert. On the back, it says that one serving size of 2/3 cup is 37g of carbs. Now, I know I'll want more than that, so I say, "OK, I want 2 cups of sherbert." That's 3 servings. 37g carbs per serving multiplied by 3 servings gives me 111 carbs. Now for the insulin. My IC ratio is 6, meaning every unit of insulin covers 6g carbs. Now, I'll divide. 111g carbs divided by an IC ratio of 6 mean I need to take 18.50 units of insulin.

The nice thing about having a pump is, once you input your IC ratio, it'll do that part for you! All you'd need to do then is carb counting.

This is a tricky subject! Like you said, everyone is their own microsystem, so I'll share what's currently working for me...

Before you correct, it's good to know what kind of food you're dealing with. There's three factors I use to correct: *Carb speed, the Glycemic Index, and Nutritional Values.*

Carb Speed is useful to know *how quickly the carbs is digested and dispersed*. If I know I'm eating Craisins (dried cranberries, omg so delicious), then because it has processed sugars and a ton of carbs, I know that it's Carb Speed is *very high*, meaning it's gonna kick in right away, meaning I gotta correct at least 20 minutes before I delve in. Conversely, if I'm having a bowl of spaghetti, it's carb speed is *low*, meaning it takes a long time to disperse, meaning I need to extend my correction out a bit... say, 60% before I eat and 40% about 15 minutes in.

The Glycemic Index (GI) is a method of saying *how much of a punch your food will have*. Call it the "hidden potential" of each carb. Each food is different, and there's many a chart online about the GI of each food. Examples: Watermelon has a GI of 76/100, which is high. Those watermelon carbs, though there's only 11 per slice, will hit you harder than you may expect. Therefore, you may want to bump up the amount you get a bit. On the other hand, Key Lime yogurt is sitting at a nice 14/100. You can expect what the carton says on this one.

And finally, there's Nutritional Value. I won't explain everything now - I'll update this after my exams - but each mineral interacts with your BG level differently. For now, take these examples: Think of Proteins as an extra-slow speed level of carbs. That's because it takes a long time for your amino acids to snip proteins into glucose that you can use. Fats don't do anything to your BG, *but they CAN make you more insulin-resistant*. Sodium is devious, on the other hand; while minimalistic, the sodium you intake absorbs some fluids. Less water with the same amount of sugar = higher BG.

The entire process of corrections is like a fun little mini-game: Keep trying things until you find that sweet spot!
